dcDescription: It is a grave find from the 7th-8th century. The function was probably that of adornment of a garment.The term 'Coptic textile' is used for fabrics found in Egyptian tombs from the Roman, Coptic and early Islamic periods (ca. 2nd-9th centuries AD). In the first centuries of this period it was customary to bury the dead in their daily clothing. Later on, people started using special, expensive burial cloths. Because of the dry soil and the preservative effect of the wood of the coffin, originating from sycomore, a wild fig tree, many fabrics have been found in good condition. A large part of the excavated garments and tissue fragments consists of linen and woollen shirts (tunica) decorated with bands (clavi) and round and square banding. These bands and trims are usually made of wool in tapestry technique (Arabic: qabati).

dataProvider: National Museum of World Cultures Foundation
dcDescription: Scarf or veil made of tulle-bi-telli fabric.\nTulle-bi-telli is a type of embroidery in which loosely woven cotton or linen (tulle) is embroidered with narrow metal strips, usually of silver or gold alloy. The embroidered fabric was made by women in the city of Asyut. In the 19th century, Egyptian women wore clothes made of this fabric during their weddings (Devine and Westerfield 2014: 46-49).In the late 19th century, when European and American tourism to Egypt boomed, tulle-bi-telli became a popular souvenir for travelers, especially in the form of shawls. The shimmering textile fitted in well with the oriental trend. In American belly-dance films, a popular film genre in the first half of the 20th century, dancers often wore costumes made of tulle-bi-telli. Egyptian belly dancers also began to use the fabric in their costumes at this time.

Sjaal of sluier van tulle-bi-telli stof.

Tulle-bi-telli is een type borduurwerk waarbij losjes geweven katoen of linnen (tule) geborduurd wordt met smalle metalen stroken, meestal van zilver- of goudlegering. De geborduurde stof werd door vrouwen in de stad Asyut vervaardigd. In de 19e eeuw droegen Egyptische vrouwen kleding van deze stof tijdens hun bruiloft (Devine and Westerfield 2014: 46-49).

Eind 19e eeuw, toen het Europees en Amerikaans toerisme naar Egypte een grote vlucht nam werd tulle-bi-telli een geliefd souvenir voor reizigers, vooral in de vorm van shawls. Het glinsterende textiel paste goed bij de oriëntalistische trend. In Amerikaanse buikdansfilms, een populair filmgenre in de eerste helft van de 20e eeuw, droegen danseressen vaak kostuums van tulle-bi-telli. Ook Egyptische buikdanseressen begonnen in deze periode de stof in hun kostuums te verwerken.
